title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
applicability_note: All APRA-regulated entities; foreign entity obligations apply to Australian branch operations
plain_language_summary: CPS 230 is APRA's single, cross-industry standard for operational risk. It asks every APRA-regulated entity to do three things well: manage operational risk through effective controls, monitoring and timely remediation; keep critical operations running through a disruption, with board-approved tolerance levels for how long an outage can last, how much data can be lost and what minimum service must continue; and manage the risks that come from relying on material service providers, which are the providers an entity depends on for a critical operation or that expose it to material operational risk. It replaced the older standards that handled outsourcing and business continuity separately. The board is ultimately accountable for all three. Notification obligations are tight: 72 hours for an operational incident with material impact, 24 hours for a disruption to a critical operation beyond tolerance, and 20 business days to notify a material service arrangement for a critical operation. The standard commenced on 1 July 2025. APRA finalised targeted amendments on 30 April 2026, and the amended version commences on 1 July 2026. Those amendments give limited exemptions from specific contractual requirements where compliance is not practicable, for material arrangements with seven categories of non-traditional service provider: government agencies, regulators, central banks, financial market exchanges, operators of clearing and settlement facilities, operators of payment systems and schemes, and financial messaging infrastructures. CPG 230 and the material service provider register template were updated to match. Transitional relief for pre-existing service provider contracts runs to the earlier of contract renewal or 1 July 2026.
why_it_matters: Models run on data, systems and third-party platforms, so model failures are often operational failures. CPS 230 is the closest thing APRA has to a home for model-related process risk: model inventories, data pipelines, vendor models and the controls around them all sit inside its operational risk and service provider requirements. Understanding CPS 230 is a practical first step toward understanding how an Australian bank would govern model risk today.
who_it_applies_to: All APRA-regulated entities: authorised deposit-taking institutions (banks, building societies, credit unions), general insurers, life insurers, private health insurers and RSE licensees (superannuation trustees). Requirements are applied proportionately, with some extra obligations for significant financial institutions.

title: APS 220 Credit Risk Management
plain_language_summary: APS 220 sets APRA's expectations for how banks identify, measure, monitor and control credit risk. A bank must have a credit risk management framework that includes a board-approved credit risk appetite and strategy (reviewed at least annually), a dedicated credit risk management function, adequate management information systems and independent review. Lending decisions must focus mainly on the borrower's capacity to repay, including under stressed conditions such as higher interest rates, rather than relying on collateral. Exposures must be classified as performing or non-performing (90+ days past due or unlikely to repay), provisions must follow Australian Accounting Standards, and problem loans need early identification and a workout process kept separate from origination. APG 220 is the companion practice guide that explains how APRA expects these requirements to be met.
why_it_matters: Credit risk is where most bank models live: probability of default, loss given default, application scorecards and expected credit loss provisioning models all feed decisions that APS 220 governs. The standard's emphasis on serviceability buffers and stress testing is a direct link between credit policy and quantitative modelling.
who_it_applies_to: All authorised deposit-taking institutions except purchased payment facility providers. Foreign ADIs must comply with most requirements.

title: APRA letter to industry on artificial intelligence (AI) risk management
plain_language_summary: In April 2026 APRA wrote to banks, insurers and superannuation trustees calling for a step-change in how AI-related risks are managed. The letter sets expectations in four areas. Boards should have enough AI literacy to oversee AI use and set strategy within risk appetite, with monitoring and defined triggers for action. Governance frameworks should cover the full AI lifecycle, with clear ownership, staff training, an inventory of AI use cases and human involvement in high-risk decisions. Supplier risk should be managed by mapping dependencies and securing contractual transparency, auditability and assurance over AI services, including concentration risk. Change management and assurance should be integrated across cyber, data governance and model performance, with monitoring proportionate to how critical each use case is.
why_it_matters: APRA does not have a single, dedicated model risk management standard. Model-related expectations are spread across capital standards that allow internal models (for example APS 113 for internal ratings-based credit risk, APS 116 for market risk and APS 117 for interest rate risk in the banking book), the risk management standard CPS 220, CPS 230 and supervisory letters like this one. This letter is the clearest recent statement of what APRA expects for inventories, lifecycle governance and ongoing performance monitoring, which are core model risk management practices.
who_it_applies_to: APRA-regulated banks, insurers and superannuation trustees that use or plan to use AI.

title: Basel Committee minimum capital requirements for market risk (FRTB)
applicability_note: Not live in Australia; EU temporary relief from 1 January 2027 for three years
plain_language_summary: The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) is the Basel Committee's rewrite of how banks calculate capital for market risk. It draws a clearer boundary between the trading book and the banking book, replaces Value-at-Risk with Expected Shortfall in the internal models approach, adds a capital charge for risk factors that cannot be modelled reliably (non-modellable risk factors), and requires trading desks to pass profit-and-loss attribution and backtesting tests to keep using internal models. A revised standardised approach acts as a credible fallback, and a simplified version is available for banks with small trading books. The January 2019 standard originally took effect from 1 January 2022; the Basel Committee deferred this to 1 January 2023 in March 2020. National implementation has been uneven: in June 2026 the European Commission adopted temporary relief measures intended to apply from 1 January 2027 for three years.
why_it_matters: FRTB is the reference framework for modern market risk capital and model approval. Its desk-level model tests (P&L attribution, backtesting) are practical examples of model validation embedded in regulation. In Australia, the current APS 116 (commenced 1 January 2025) still uses the earlier standard method and internal model approach; APRA's February 2023 policy priorities said it would consult on revised market risk standards and push effective dates to 2026, so check APRA's latest policy priorities for the current timeline before relying on any date.
who_it_applies_to: Internationally active banks in Basel Committee member jurisdictions, as implemented by each national regulator. In Australia, ADIs with trading book activity are covered by APS 116.

title: US revised guidance on model risk management (SR 26-2)
applicability_note: Most relevant above USD 30b in total assets
plain_language_summary: On 17 April 2026 the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC jointly issued revised model risk management guidance. For the Federal Reserve it is SR 26-2, which supersedes SR 11-7 (2011), the document that shaped model risk practice worldwide for more than a decade, and SR 21-8 on BSA/AML models. The new guidance is more principles-based. It narrows the definition of a model to complex quantitative methods grounded in statistical, economic or financial theory, excluding simple calculations and deterministic rule-based processes. It is described as most relevant to banking organisations with more than USD 30 billion in assets. Generative and agentic AI are outside its scope, with the agencies signalling separate future work. Three changes matter most for practice. Materiality, set by model purpose together with model exposure, now drives how much oversight a model gets, and an immaterial model can be monitored rather than fully validated. SR 11-7's at-least-annual validation cadence and its prescriptive board approval and annual policy review are not carried over; validators need "sufficient independence to maintain objectivity" rather than a prescribed reporting line. Vendor model expectations are lighter, with the explicit contingency planning requirement removed. The guidance also states plainly that it does not set enforceable standards and that non-compliance will not by itself draw supervisory criticism.
why_it_matters: SR 11-7 was the global reference point for model risk management, including in Australian banks that had no dedicated APRA standard to follow. Its replacement changes the benchmark: less prescription on validation structure and independence, a narrower model definition and a higher size threshold. Anyone describing 'SR 11-7 practices' in an interview should know it has now been superseded.
who_it_applies_to: US banking organisations supervised by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC, primarily those above USD 30 billion in total assets, and smaller institutions with significant model risk.

title: PRA SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
applicability_note: Firms with internal model approval (IRB, IMA or IMM); applied proportionately
plain_language_summary: SS1/23 sets out five principles for model risk management: (1) model identification and model risk classification, (2) governance, (3) model development, implementation and use, (4) independent model validation, and (5) model risk mitigants. Firms must keep a model inventory, tier models by risk, assign overall responsibility for model risk management to a senior manager, and report regularly to the board audit committee on how effective it is. The principles are applied proportionately. The PRA published an updated version on 23 April 2026.
why_it_matters: SS1/23 is one of the clearest current statements of what a complete model risk management framework looks like, and its five principles map neatly onto the categories used in this platform's self-assessment tool.
who_it_applies_to: UK-incorporated banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with approval to use internal models for regulatory capital (IRB, IMA or IMM).

title: OSFI Guideline E-23 Model Risk Management (2027)
applicability_note: All federally regulated financial institutions; applied proportionately
plain_language_summary: Canada's banking and insurance regulator finalised a revised model risk guideline in September 2025, taking effect on 1 May 2027. It expects enterprise-wide model risk management built around three outcomes: model risk is understood across the organisation with senior management oversight; governance intensity scales with each model's risk rating, supported by a complete inventory; and controls cover the full lifecycle from design and review through deployment, monitoring and decommissioning. It explicitly brings AI and machine learning models into scope, with extra attention to explainability, bias and autonomous decision-making.
why_it_matters: E-23 shows where model risk regulation is heading: risk-tiered, lifecycle-based and inclusive of AI. It is a useful contrast with the US approach in SR 26-2, which leaves generative and agentic AI out of scope.
who_it_applies_to: All federally regulated financial institutions in Canada, including banks, foreign bank branches, life and property and casualty insurers, and trust and loan companies, applied proportionately.

title: APS 116 Capital Adequacy: Market Risk (and APG 116)
applicability_note: ADIs with trading book activity or foreign exchange or commodity positions; foreign ADIs and purchased payment facility providers are excluded
plain_language_summary: APS 116 sets how much capital an Australian bank must hold for traded market risk, foreign exchange and commodities. The current version commenced on 1 January 2025. A bank uses the standard method, an internal model approach with APRA's approval, or a combination of the two with approval. The standard method assigns prescribed charges by risk type: interest rate risk through a maturity or duration ladder with separate specific and general market risk charges, 8 per cent for equity specific and general risk, 8 per cent of the net open foreign exchange position and of gold, and 15 per cent plus a spread charge for commodities. The internal model approach is still the pre-FRTB framework: daily capital is based on a 60-day average Value-at-Risk scaled by a multiplier of at least 3.0 plus the previous day's VaR, the same again for stressed VaR, an incremental risk charge for specific risk, and a comprehensive risk measure for correlation trading. The multiplier carries a plus factor of 0 to 1 driven by backtesting exceptions. Model use needs APRA approval, must continue once approved unless APRA revokes or suspends it, and material model changes need prior written approval. Counterparty credit risk capital sits outside this standard: paragraph 8 sends it to APS 112 or APS 113, depending on which credit risk approach the bank uses. APG 116 is the companion practice guide.
why_it_matters: This is where Australian market risk capital actually lives, and it is the clearest example of the gap between Basel and the Australian rulebook. The Basel Committee's FRTB replaced VaR with Expected Shortfall and added P&L attribution tests, but the APS 116 in force here still runs VaR, stressed VaR and the incremental risk charge. APRA's published market risk review page still shows the October 2021 timeline, which pointed at a 1 January 2025 commencement for the FRTB-aligned standards, and that did not happen, so there is no current public implementation date. If you are asked in an interview how Australia handles market risk capital, the accurate answer is that FRTB is not live here yet and APS 116 remains a Basel 2.5-style framework, with the timeline to be confirmed from APRA's latest policy priorities.
who_it_applies_to: All authorised deposit-taking institutions except foreign ADIs, purchased payment facility providers, and ADIs with no trading book activity and no foreign exchange or commodity positions.
